Growing is a series of steps, each taken when the numbers call for it: before launch, around fifty thousand users, around half a million, and a million and above.

Before launch: a managed database with daily backups.
A managed database with backups.

when: what happens at fifty thousand users
replies: At about fifty thousand users: photos move to file storage, a proper product search index, lists loaded a page at a time, and monitoring with alerts.
File storage, better search, paged lists and monitoring.

when: what happens at half a million
replies: At about half a million users: several servers behind a load balancer, a connection pooler, a read-only database copy, a job queue, and load testing.
More servers, a read copy, a job queue and load tests.

when: what happens at a million users
replies: At a million and above: bigger database machines with a standby, data split by region, a content delivery network, and perhaps a larger cloud.
Bigger machines, regional data and a larger cloud.

when: why not build for millions now
replies: Each step costs money every month, so it's taken when the numbers call for it, not all at once.
Steps are taken only when they're needed.
Usually only a small share of users are on at the same moment. The design allows many servers side by side to share the load.
Yes, by running more servers side by side.
The server keeps no memory of who's signed in, so many copies can run side by side. The data is in PostgreSQL, and each region is its own marketplace.
Stateless servers, PostgreSQL, and regions kept separate.
DigitalOcean today. At very large size, moving to a larger cloud is an option, and the code moves unchanged.
DigitalOcean now, larger clouds possible later.
Medway first, then other areas, then countries such as Nigeria and Kenya, each as its own marketplace.
Medway, then more of the UK, then abroad.
